paper_title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: 3 5 (cid:131) 6 2 4 1 12 11 10 31 12 (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) (cid:131) Understanding human motion is fundamental for science, and for AI systems that interact with, assist, or learn from humans (Yin et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Bonnetto et al., 2026). Recently, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong abilities to perceive and reason about human activity from video, yet largely from third-person perspective (Li et al., 2024a; Qi et al., 2026). Egocentric video, captured from first-person perspective using wearable devices, offers fundamentally different viewpoint, central to augmented reality interfaces, wearable assistants, and embodied agents (Yang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025b; Bonnetto et al., 2026). However, this viewpoint introduces distinct challenges (Grauman et al., 2022; He et al., 2025). First, the actors body and actions are often only partially visible to the camera, despite being essential for understanding the wearers intention and activity. Second, fine-grained motion dynamics, such as repetition counts or movement direction, are often hard to perceive from the egocentric view. Finally, motion blur and rapid viewpoint changes are common in egocentric video, requiring MLLMs to integrate ego-motion cues across frames. Fine-grained body-motion understanding from an egocentric view is therefore challenging task. Yet existing egocentric video benchmarks (e.g., (Mangalam et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2022; Bonnetto et al., 2025)) target other dimensions of video understanding, such as long-form video comprehension or domain-specific, goal-oriented task reasoning  (Table 1)  . None directly measures whether model can infer the moving body itself: its configuration at moment and the way its actions unfold over time. As result, it remains unclear whether progress on egocentric video reflects understanding of human motion or recognition of the objects and scenes in which motion takes place. To fill this gap, we introduce SOMA (Greek for body), multimodal benchmark for fine-grained understanding of human body motion and behavior from egocentric video. SOMA evaluates MLLMs on 12 tasks organized into three capability axes that mirror the aforementioned challenges: Body Configuration, Motion Dynamics, and Temporal Reasoning, which probe how the body is configured, how it moves, and how its actions unfold in time. As source for egocentric videos with annotations, we selected two comprehensive corpora, Nymeria (Ma et al., 2024) and Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024). Based on tailored pipeline including human verification, we derived final benchmark of 1,632 multiple-choice questions. We additionally release SOMA-Train, multimodal training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, combination absent from existing egocentric video benchmarks  (Table 1)  . We evaluated 37 leading MLLMs on SOMA, spanning closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric systems. Furthermore, five human evaluators independently answered all 1,632 questions, requiring over 450 hours of manual labor. The best-performing model, Qwen3.6-27B, reaches only 50.0% zero-shot accuracy, well below the 68.5% mean accuracy achieved by humans. This gap persists even with denser temporal sampling and explicit test-time reasoning, which yield only limited, model-dependent gains. Error analysis shows that the most common failures stem from misreading the wearers own body, along with difficulty localizing events in time. Motivated by this, we test whether an explicit body-motion signal helps: fine-tuning on SOMA-Train with aligned video and motion yields modest gains, suggesting that body motion can provide information complementary to video, paving the way toward developing MLLMs that better perceive human motion.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Human Motion Understanding. Understanding human motion is long-standing problem (Aggarwal & Cai, 1999), studied through various approaches. One line of work focuses on perception: methods reconstruct 3D body pose from video (Goel et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026b) and operate on skeleton inputs to recognize and segment human actions (Duan et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2024; Stoffl et al., 2024). complementary line of work studies motion generation, modeling the distribution of plausible motions to synthesize new ones from text (Guo et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025). In contemporary work, MLLMs treat motion as modality alongside text, unifying motion comprehension and generation within single model (Wu et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c). Yet, models that explicitly combine video and body motion remain uncommon, with few publicly available implementations and model weights. Furthermore, these MLLMs focus on the exocentric setting, where occlusions are rare and motion-capture data is more straightforward. To address this, SOMA evaluates how well current MLLMs perceive body motion from first-person video, complementing the body-motion benchmarks that operate on third-person or motion-capture input alone  (Table 1)  . MLLMs for Video Understanding. Building on the success of large language models (Achiam et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025a; Cai et al., 2024), MLLMs extend text-only systems to additional modalities (Han et al., 2024; Girdhar et al., 2022; Comanici et al., 2025). Among these, video MLLMs (Li et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Qi et al., 2026) address the understanding and reasoning of video content. Motivated by applications in AR, robotics, and assistive systems, separate line of work adapts MLLMs to the egocentric setting. For example, EgoThinker (Pei et al., 2025) enhances egocentric reasoning through chain-of-thought rationales, and EgoGPT (Yang et al., 2025b) fine-tunes video MLLM for egocentric captioning and QA. However, existing egocentric MLLMs remain optimized for activityand scene-level understanding, leaving the question of fine-grained body-motion perception largely unexplored. SOMA is designed to evaluate this capability explicitly, exposing the shortcomings of current models, while also providing training split to further advance their development. Egocentric VQA Benchmarks. Egocentric video question-answering is expanding rapidly across several directions. Early benchmarks established the format for first-person video QA, with EgoTaskQA (Jia et al., 2022) probing goal-oriented task understanding and EgoSchema (Mangalam et al., 2023) targeting long-form video. More recent benchmarks explore specific aspects of egocentric understanding, including first-person perspective thinking (Cheng et al., 2024), cross-domain and domain-specific understanding (Bonnetto et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026), and temporal reasoning (Plizzari et al., 2025). Despite this breadth, none of these benchmarks target the perception of the moving human body. Specifically, tasks such as activity recognition, task planning, and temporal grounding remain focused on objects and the surrounding environment, rather than the body itself. We fill this gap by introducing body-centric question taxonomy grounded in fine-grained bodymotion annotations, paired with video and 3D body pose, which probes competencies that existing benchmarks do not directly evaluate  (Table 1)  .

sections.title: 3 THE SOMA BENCHMARK
sections.content: We introduce SOMA, multimodal benchmark for fine-grained understanding of human body motion from egocentric videos. We describe the task suite (Sec. 3.1), the data curation pipeline (Sec. 3.2), dataset statistics (Sec. 3.3), and our training dataset SOMA-Train (Sec. 3.4).

sections.title: 3.1 TASK SUITE
sections.content: We organize the benchmark around three axes, each targeting one of the aforementioned challenges: Body Configuration, Motion Dynamics, and Temporal Reasoning. Together, they comprise 12 tasks that span distinct competencies in understanding moving body from the first-person view (Figure 2). Body Configuration. These tasks probe perception of the body and its parts during an activity. Hand Use identifies which hand performs given action. Bimanual Coordination characterizes how the two hands act together, including their role assignment and consistency across repeated instances. Body Posture identifies the persons overall posture at specified moment or window. Concurrent Body-Part State identifies what one body part is doing given the activity of another.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 2: SOMA Benchmark Taxonomy. SOMA comprises 12 tasks organized into three capability axes: Body Configuration, Motion Dynamics and Temporal Reasoning. We show the distribution of questions across tasks, together with representative question for each task. See Appendix for more examples. Motion Dynamics. This axis tests perception of fine-grained motion. Repetition Counting enumerates the occurrences of specified repetitive motion. Movement Direction identifies the direction of motion, turning, or short navigation sequence. Opposite Motion Discrimination distinguishes semantically opposed motions such as push and pull, open and close, that share visual context but differ in motion polarity. Temporal Reasoning. This axis groups tasks that require reasoning about how motion-grounded events unfold over time, including their relationships and progression. Adjacent Action Identification identifies the action immediately preceding or following reference event. Chronological Ordering places three or more actions in their correct temporal order. Missing Event Inference infers the missing intermediate action between two anchoring events. Next Action Prediction predicts the action following trimmed clip, requiring inference of an unobserved action. Repeated Event Reasoning identifies what occurs after specified occurrence of repeated event.

sections.title: 3.2 DATA CURATION PIPELINE
sections.content: We construct SOMA through multi-stage pipeline: sourcing data and task assignment, question generation, filtering, and human review (Figure 3). We describe each stage below. Sourcing Data and Task Assignment. We sourced videos from Nymeria (Ma et al., 2024) and Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024), two egocentric corpora that span wide range of real-world domains with rich action and body motion annotations. Both corpora provide atomic action annotations = {(aj, τj)}, where aj is detailed natural-language action description and τj = [ts j] its temporal interval. Nymeria additionally provides motion narrations = {(pj, hj, ℓj, τj)}, finegrained descriptions of body posture pj, hand motion hj, and leg motion ℓj over the same interval. These narrations are central to SOMA, as they describe body state and movement in natural language, which supports our body-centric question generation. Not every domain, however, supports every task equally; therefore, we discarded domaintask pairs that would produce trivial question, such as asking about hand use during an activity where the hands are idle. j, te Question and Answer Generation. Our question generation procedure consists of two steps. First, an LLM selector receives the relevant textual annotation streams for video (drawn from and M) and identifies sub-sequence specifically relevant to the task. For example, for Bimanual Coordination, it identifies segment in which both hands are simultaneously active. The annotation streams from the selected segment are then passed as input to an LLM generator, which produces multiple-choice question with one correct answer and three task-specific distractors. This two-step design narrows the context before question construction, so each example is grounded in task-relevant annotations. We implemented both modules with Gemini 2.5 Flash and manually designed detailed prompts with step-by-step instructions and in-context examples for each task (Appendix B.1), producing 3,928 candidate questions. The only exception to this step is Repetition Counting, as exact counts of fine-grained motions cannot be reliably extracted from the narrations, and we found it more effective to create the questions and counts manually (Appendix B.3).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 3: SOMA Data Construction Pipeline. We construct SOMA through task assignment, taskspecific question generation, and quality control with blind-filtering and human validation. Blind-Language Filtering. Modern LLMs carry substantial prior knowledge and can often answer questions correctly without seeing the video. central goal of SOMA is to test whether models can perceive body motion in egocentric video, so questions answerable from language alone undermine the benchmark. To identify such questions, we apply blind-language filter: four models (Gemini 2.5 Flash (Comanici et al., 2025), GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-72B (Yang et al., 2024), and InternVL3-78B (Zhu et al., 2025b)) answer each question without video, and we remove questions answered correctly by at least two solvers (Appendix B.4). This step removed 45.9% of the questions, leaving 2,127 for human review and concentrating the benchmark on questions that cannot be reliably solved from language priors and require visual understanding. Human Review. Finally, to verify the correctness and quality of every remaining question, human reviewer inspects each question through custom interface that streams the source video segment alongside synchronized 3D body-pose rendering, used as an additional reference for validation. For each question, the reviewer chooses to accept, modify (its text, options, or segment bounds), or delete it, to minimize question ambiguity, so that the final benchmark contains only high-quality, verified questions (Appendix B.4).

sections.title: 3.3 DATASET STATISTICS
sections.content: SOMA consists of 1,632 multiple-choice questions that span 12 tasks across three axes (Figure 2). The questions are drawn from 397 unique videos, producing 1,611 clips that span diverse everyday scenarios. The average length is 35.6 seconds with most concentrated between 10 and 60 seconds. Body Configuration and Motion Dynamics clips fall mainly within this range, reflecting the shortterm nature of body-motion cues, while Temporal Reasoning clips extend further into the long tail. Answer distributions are balanced across options to mitigate position bias.

sections.title: 3.4 SOMA-TRAIN
sections.content: To facilitate further investigation and motivate future research in the domain, we introduce training split, SOMA-Train, which comprises aligned egocentric video, body-motion, and language supervision. We adapted the benchmark generation pipeline (Sec. 3.2), without human verification, and constructed 28,596 question-answer pairs over 110.2 hours of aligned video and body motion, while keeping the training data disjoint from the SOMA evaluation set at the participant and scene level. Since existing Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024) body-motion fits are provided at 10 fps and cover only part of the videos, we follow Patel et al. (2025) to reconstruct 3D body motion at 20 fps from the multi-view recordings. We detail the construction, debiasing method, and motion processing in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Human Performance. To contextualize model performance, we measure human accuracy without prior familiarity with the benchmark. Five compensated evaluators, none of whom took part in data annotation, independently answered all 1,632 questions, totaling over 450 hours of evaluation. We report their mean accuracy as an estimate of human-level performance on this task.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Evaluation Setup. We evaluate 37 leading MLLMs spanning closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric systems (Table 2 and Appendix C.2). We report per-task and overall accuracy (%), using lmms-eval (Zhang et al., 2025b), standard multimodal evaluation framework, to ensure consistent evaluation and facilitate future comparisons. Unless otherwise specified, models are evaluated zero-shot with temperature set to 0 and uniformly sampled 16 frames per segment to balance computational cost and comparability across models with different context lengths. We also ablate key evaluation settings (Sec. 5.2). Further implementation details, including prompt templates, are provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We first compare MLLMs with human performance across the SOMA tasks (Sec. 5.1) and examine the effect of inference-time strategies (Sec. 5.2). We then analyze common failure modes (Sec. 5.3) and study whether combining video and body-motion signals can improve performance (Sec. 5.4).

sections.title: 5.1 MLLM AND HUMAN PERFORMANCE ON SOMA
sections.content: All evaluated models struggle on SOMA, and no model reaches human performance. The best model, Qwen3.6-27B, reaches 50.0% average accuracy, and the best closed-source model, Gemini 3.5 Flash, reaches 47.0%, well below the human average of 68.5%  (Table 2)  . The gap, however, is not uniform. Compared with the best model per task, it is largest on Repetition Counting (45.3 points), Repeated Event Reasoning (25.4), and Bimanual Coordination (25.3), whereas it closes or reverses on Concurrent Body-Part State (1.1) and Next Action Prediction (10.0). The difference in these tasks lies in whether the answer is present in the video or must be inferred. In Concurrent Body-Part State, the queried body part is often outside the field of view, and in Next Action Prediction, the action has not yet occurred. Since both humans and models must infer the answer, humans have little advantage on these tasks. In contrast, on the other tasks, the relevant cues are present in the video but are subtle or spread over time. While humans rely on these cues, we find that current models fail to use them reliably. Performance is uneven across tasks. Models perform best on tasks where the evidence is concentrated in few frames and can be directly observed, such as Hand Use and Opposite Motion Discrimination, where the best models reach 74.6% and 71.4%, respectively. In contrast, performance drops when the answer requires following the motion across the clip: on Chronological Ordering and Repeated Event Reasoning, most models score below 40%. This indicates that current MLLMs are better at recognizing frame-level cues than at integrating body motion over time. Egocentric specialization alone is not sufficient. Despite being adapted to egocentric video, the three specialized models do not outperform general-purpose open-source models of similar size. This suggests gap in current egocentric models when it comes to body-motion perception, consistent with their training data, which focuses primarily on actions, objects, and intentions, with no dedicated supervision of whole-body posture or motion. Addressing this limitation will likely require egocentric models that are more robust and more sensitive to fine-grained body dynamics. Increasing model size improves performance, but larger models still fall short. Qwen3-VL gains 13.1 points from 2B to 32B, and Qwen3.5 gains 17.8 points from 0.8B to 27B, while InternVL3.5 improves by 8.1 points from 1B to 38B and is not monotonic. Larger backbones therefore help on SOMA, but scaling alone does not close the gap to human performance, and the largest models tested remain far from saturating the benchmark. 5.2 IMPACT OF TEMPORAL SAMPLING AND TEST-TIME REASONING Effect of Temporal Sampling Density. To study how temporal sampling affects performance, we evaluate nine models on 1 to 64 uniformly sampled input frames (Figure 4A). Accuracy increases when moving from single to multiple frames but saturates quickly. Averaged across models, it rises by 5.4 points from 1 to 16 frames, while adding frames beyond 16 contributes at most an additional 0.5. The magnitude of this gain is strongly model-dependent, ranging from 1.2 points (VideoLLaMA3-7B) to 10.3 points (Qwen3.5-9B) between 1 and 16 frames. Temporal sampling density is therefore not the principal limitation. Beyond access to visual evidence on the order of tens of frames, what models lack is the ability to integrate that evidence across time.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Effect of Test-Time Reasoning. We next ask whether explicit test-time reasoning, effective on many language reasoning tasks, also helps with visual reasoning, specifically body-motion perception in video. We compare the performance change after enabling thinking for instruction-tuned models, or after switching to their thinking variant (Qwen3-VL-8B and Kimi-VL-A3B), under each models recommended sampling parameters. The effect is strongly model-dependent (Figure 4B). Five models improve by at least one point, all from the Qwen3.53.8 family, with gains of 1.0 to 10.2 points, while the remaining seven either show negligible change or decline. Test-time reasoning is therefore not sufficient solution for closing the humanmodel gap: simply encouraging thinking in current reasoning mechanisms does not address their limitations in perceiving body motion.

sections.title: 5.3 QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE ERROR ANALYSIS
sections.content: The nature of some questions allows us to explicitly quantify model errors, which we complement with qualitative analysis of reasoning traces. Models show strong right-hand bias on handedness questions. We split each handedness question by its correct answer and measure per-class accuracy. Averaged across the 37 models of Table 2, accuracy reaches 78.8% for right hand but drops to 44.3% for left hand (Appendix D.4.2), on question that is, in principle, visually unambiguous: the five human annotators are equally accurate on both classes (mean accuracy of 92.7% left, 89.8% right). This asymmetry is consistent with prior inherited from pretraining data: since roughly 90% of the human population is righthanded (Papadatou-Pastou et al., 2020), right-handed actions are over-represented in the video-text corpora used to train MLLMs, and models default to right when the visual evidence is weak. Most models lean toward under-counting. Repetition counting shows the largest humanmodel gap in SOMA (88.9% for humans against 43.6% for the best model on this task), so we look more closely at how models fail, classifying each incorrect prediction as an under-count (below the true count) or an over-count (above the true count). In total, 24 of the 37 evaluated models lean toward under-counting, consistent with frame-sampling explanation: repetitions falling between sampled frames are simply missed, biasing the count downward. The asymmetry is nonetheless strongly model-dependent, indicating that beyond the shared sampling bottleneck, individual models apply their own priors when they cannot directly enumerate repetitions (Appendix D.4.3). Errors in Reasoning Traces. To better understand the limitations of current MLLMs, we analyze the errors made in their reasoning traces. We focus on Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B, the latest models from the two leading opensource families on SOMA, and select 200 questions, stratified across tasks, that both models answered incorrectly. By inspecting the wrong predictions, we identify four primary error types: 1) Visual Grounding Errors involve misidentifying the objects, scenes, or people involved; 2) Motion and Body-State Perception Errors involve incorrectly perceiving the wearers own movement, posture, or limb use; 3) Temporal Localization Errors involve placing correctly identified events at the wrong point in time; and 4) Prior-Driven Inference Errors involve answering from expectation rather than visual evidence. Further details, including the annotation procedure and qualitative examples of each error type, are provided in Appendix D.4. Figure 5: Distribution of Error Types. Root causes of incorrect answers across two representative MLLMs. Motion and body-state perception is the dominant error for both models on Body Configuration and Motion Dynamics, indicating that most failures on these axes stem from misreading the wearers own body, including misjudging their posture, the limb in use, or the direction of their movement (examples in Appendix D.4.1). In addition, models also struggle with temporal localization, showing difficulty in tracking the wearers dynamics over time and in correct order. Visual grounding and prior-driven inference account for smaller shares of failures across all three axes, reflecting difficulties in identifying the relevant visual information and tendency to favor plausible over ob-

sections.title: 5.4 TRAINING BODY-AWARE MLLMS
sections.content: We found that MLLMs fail most when they need to perceive the wearers body, which is hard to infer from egocentric vision. Humans do not rely on vision only: other exteroceptive and proprioceptive signals complement vision (vestibular, muscle spindles and tactile) and provide continuous estimate of ones own posture and movement (Proske & Gandevia, 2012). This raises natural question: if model is given comparable signal, stream of body-motion information alongside the video, does it perceive and reason better? We investigated this by extending two openweight MLLM backbones, Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025) and InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025), with body-motion pathway following the standard LLaVA/MotionLLM design (Liu et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025): frozen VQVAE motion encoder (Zhang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2022) was used to extract continuous latents, which were projected into the languagemodel embedding space and inserted as motion tokens in the input sequence (see Appendix E.3 for architecture, training curriculum, and hyperparameters). We fine-tuned each backbone on SOMA-Train (Appendix E) in three input settings, motion-only, video-only, and video+motion, and evaluated them on SOMA against the zero-shot video-only backbone  (Table 3)  . Motion-only fine-tuned MLLMs already perform above chance, suggesting that body motion is informative on its own, though performance remains low: motion alone is often insufficient to infer visual content, such as surrounding scenes or objects. For comparison, existing motiononly models evaluated zero-shot remain close to random chance on SOMA (Appendix D.5). Video fine-tuning improves both backbones well above zero-shot performance. Adding aligned motion provides further but modest improvement for both backbones. However, the effect varies across capability axes: motion slightly improves Body Configuration and Temporal Reasoning for both backbones, while on Motion Dynamics it helps Qwen3-VL-8B but slightly hurts InternVL3.5-8B (see Appendix E.4 for task-level results). We also found results consistent with these findings when ablating video/motion modalities at test time  (Table 12)  . Overall, these results suggest that body motion can provide information complementary to the visual signal, but that its benefits depend on the task and remain limited for the provided, vanilla baselines. This motivates future research on multimodal sensory integration.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced SOMA, benchmark for fine-grained understanding of human body motion in egocentric video, spanning 12 tasks across three capability axes. Across closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric models, we found large gap to human performance, showing that perceiving the moving body from first-person view remains an open problem. We see natural parallel to the human brain, where visual input from the eyes is complemented by multiple sensors (tactile, vestibular, proprioceptive) to form coherent representation of the subject and its environment (Blanke, 2012; Bonnetto et al., 2026). In egocentric video, the body is largely unseen, so model must likewise infer posture, locomotion, and actions from indirect evidence such as hand pose and ego-motion. We found that current MLLMs underperform in this capacity. We hope that SOMA motivates the development of multimodal systems that better pair first-person video with motion signals to acquire the body awareness current models lack and that systems meant to assist, instruct, or learn from humans will ultimately require. We note that beyond MLLMs, emerging world models (Matsuo et al., 2022) might be ideally suited for this challenge.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In the preparation of this manuscript, we used generative AI tools for writing assistance. The primary purpose of their use was to aid in editing and polishing the writing of this paper to improve clarity and readability, such as improving grammar and refining sentence structure. All research ideas, methods, analyses, and conclusions in this paper were formulated and developed exclusively by the authors. We have manually reviewed and verified all AI-assisted edits for accuracy and take full responsibility for the final content of this work. In addition, LLMs were used as part of our benchmark construction pipeline to generate candidate question-answer pairs (Sec. 3.2), and all generated questions were human-verified.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: The ethical considerations and potential risks of this work are limited. SOMA is constructed from two existing public egocentric video datasets, Nymeria and Ego-Exo4D, collected under informedconsent protocols established by their original creators, which we enhance with human-verified novel question-answer annotations; this verification process is anonymized. We used these datasets for benchmark construction and evaluation, following their intended research use. We manually verified the generated QA to ensure quality. Our human evaluation study involved 5 paid participants, who gave informed consent and were compensated for their time. Our experiments evaluate publicly accessible MLLM systems, including released open-source checkpoints and public API models, and are limited to aggregate benchmark performance rather than deployment in real-world decisionmaking settings. Our analysis also revealed handedness bias in MLLMs, which future research could address. More broadly, while direct risks are limited, advances in egocentric body-motion understanding could support beneficial applications such as assistive technologies and robotics, but may also raise concerns around surveillance or behavioral profiling.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: The details needed to reproduce our work are provided throughout the main paper and appendix. The SOMA construction pipeline is described in Sec. 3.2, with additional details, including the exact selector, generator, and blind-filtering prompts, given in Appendix B. The human evaluation protocol is detailed in Appendix C.1. The MLLM evaluation setup is explained in Sec. 4, with specific implementation details given in Appendix C.3, together with the complete list of evaluated models in Appendix C.2 and the exact prompts used for evaluation in Appendices C.4 and C.5. The construction of our training dataset is described in Appendix E, and our fine-tuning architecture and hyperparameters are given in Appendix E.3. Code, benchmark data, and training data will be made publicly available upon paper acceptance.

[...] Cannot produce 3 distractors where at least one is successor of B.2 MITIGATING GENERATOR BIAS Benchmark questions generated by an LLM may inherit regularities of the generating model in their phrasing, answer formulation, and distractor construction, which could advantage models from the same family at evaluation time, concern analogous to self-preference in LLM-based evaluation (Panickssery et al., 2024). Since Gemini 2.5 Flash is both our generator and one of the evaluated models, we took two measures to mitigate such bias. First, the question generation stage is not an open-ended LLM writing process: the model fills fixed task-specific question templates, while both the correct answer and the distractors are derived from the ground-truth annotations under predefined rules (Appendix B.1). The generator therefore has limited freedom to introduce stylistic regularities of its own, and the resulting questions largely reflect the source annotations rather than the generating model. Second, Gemini 2.5 Flash is one of the four blind solvers in the filtering stage (Sec. 3.2). Questions that Gemini answers correctly without the video, together with at least one other blind solver, are therefore removed during construction, before any MLLM is evaluated. B.3 MANUAL ANNOTATION OF REPETITION COUNTING For each selected take, we used the 3D body-pose data to identify segments containing repetitive motion; human annotator then inspected each candidate segment, examining the video together with the synchronized 3D body-pose rendering, and created the question and recorded the count for each. One repetition is defined as single completed instance of the action named in the question. Segments containing partial repetitions, occluded repetitions, or otherwise unclear repetition boundaries are discarded rather than annotated with an uncertain count, so repetition is counted only when it is clearly visible. Examples are available in Appendix A. This adds 101 Repetition Counting questions to the candidate set.

sections.content: B.4 FILTERING AND REVIEW STATISTICS Across the eleven automatically generated tasks, our pipeline produced 3,928 candidate questions. The blind-language filter removed questions answered correctly by at least two of four solvers, using the prompt shown below. Blind Solver Prompt You are answering multiple-choice question about first-person (egocentric) video that you have NOT been shown. You will see only the question text and four options labeled A, B, C, D. Use your world knowledge, common sense, and any clues in the wording of the question itself to pick the option you think is most Commit to exactly one letter even if uncertain --- likely correct. guess if you have to. Respond with ONLY JSON object with the single key answer, whose value is one of A, B, C, D: {answer: X} Do not include any other text, explanation, markdown, or extra keys. This process removed 1,801 questions (45.9%), leaving the remaining 2,127 for human review. Removal rates were highest for Body Posture (62.4%) and Hand Use (53.7%), where the answer space is small and natural language priors were strongest, and lowest for Repeated Event Reasoning (30.8%) and Chronological Ordering (39.8%), where the correct answer depended on multi-event temporal structure that is difficult to recover from text alone. During human review, 945 questions were accepted as-is, 586 were modified, and 596 were deleted. Combined with the 101 manually annotated Repetition Counting questions (Appendix B.3), the final benchmark contains 1,632 multiple-choice questions.

sections.content: C.1 DETAILS ON HUMAN EVALUATION Human performance was measured as the average accuracy of five human subjects who were not involved in the construction or annotation of the benchmark. Each subject independently evaluated the full set of 1,632 samples. For every sample, annotators were presented with the video, question, and four answer options, and were allowed unlimited time to select the single best answer based on the visual information in the video. When the camera wearers body is not directly visible, annotators were instructed to rely on indirect visual cues, such as camera motion, viewpoint changes, and hand-object interactions. Completing the full evaluation required 89, 90, 94, 97, and 95 hours for the five annotators, respectively, corresponding to an average of 93 hours per annotator and 465 hours of human evaluation in total. Annotators were compensated for their time spent completing the evaluation. We report the standard deviation in accuracy across the five human annotators for each task  (Table 4)  . sections.content: We uniformly sampled 16 frames per video segment across all models to balance computational cost and comparability across models with different context lengths; Sec. 5.2 studies the effect of denser sampling on performance. We used lmms-eval (Zhang et al., 2025b), standardized framework for evaluating multimodal models across wide range of tasks. We instructed all models to respond with single letter corresponding to their chosen option; when response requires further parsing, we used the common method that other multiple-choice tasks in lmms-eval apply, which checks the response against set of common answer-formatting patterns to identify the selected option. All open-source model experiments were run on either 4 H100 or 4 A100 GPUs. sections.content: D.1 EFFECT OF CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT PROMPTING Test-time reasoning can also be invoked without dedicated thinking mode, by instructing model to reason step by step before answering (Wei et al., 2022). We evaluated five open-source models by extending the original prompt with CoT instruction that asks the model to observe, reason, then answer (Appendix C.5). Reasoning step-by-step did not systematically help on SOMA  (Table 5)  . Only Qwen3.8-27B benefited, gaining 3.9 points and improving on 11 of 12 tasks, with the largest gains in temporal reasoning and motion dynamics. For the remaining models, CoT had neutral effect or reduced performance. This mirrors the thinking-mode result (Figure 4) and suggests that current reasoning mechanisms do not address the difficulty of perceiving body motion, and additional reasoning tokens do little to help. Table 5: Effect of Chain-of-Thought Prompting on SOMA. Accuracy (%) across the three capability axes. sections.content: D.2 INFERENCE-TIME ANALYSIS PER CAPABILITY AXIS D.2.1 EFFECT OF TEMPORAL SAMPLING DENSITY Denser frame sampling does not help the three capability axes equally. For Body Configuration tasks, where questions ask about the bodys state at specific moment, accuracy saturates early. possible explanation is that the relevant evidence for these questions is concentrated in small number of frames, so additional frames beyond that point add little new information, even though correctly extracting that evidence remains difficult. For Motion Dynamics tasks, which ask how the body moves and are hard to answer from only few frames, accuracy continues to improve for most models, though only marginally beyond 16 frames. Temporal Reasoning remains the weakest axis at every sampling density, suggesting that regardless of how many frames the model is given, it struggles to integrate that information over time. Figure 28: Effect of temporal sampling density on accuracy, per capability axis. D.2.2 EFFECT OF TEST-TIME REASONING The effect of test-time reasoning also varies by axis. Gains are largest on Motion Dynamics, where most models improve; these tasks often require counting or distinguishing observed motion, which can benefit from explicit reasoning once the motion itself has been perceived. On Body Configuration, which is the most perceptual of the three axes, most models show negligible change or decline. Changes on Temporal Reasoning are modest overall. This suggests that reasoning helps once the relevant evidence has been observed, but does not compensate for failure to perceive it in the first place. sections.content: D.3 PERFORMANCE BY QUESTION DIFFICULTY Questions in SOMA differ in how demanding they are. To understand how models and humans perform across different difficulty levels, we adopted the concept of psychometric curves (Boring, 1917), following Qi et al. (2026). We used Gemini 2.5 Pro to rate each question from 1 (very easy) to 4 (hard) according to how difficult it is to distinguish between the options, using the prompt shown below, and we report the accuracy of every evaluated model and our human annotators at each level (Figure 30). Accuracy falls with difficulty for both humans and all models, with humans remaining far ahead at every level. The gap is largest on the easiest questions, showing that models fall short even on simple cases and across the full difficulty range of the benchmark. D.4 ERROR ANALYSIS Figure 30: Human and model performance across question difficulty levels. The human curve is the mean over five annotators with the band showing 1 SE. Here we provide the full definitions of the four error types used in Sec. 5.3, which we identified through manual inspection of subset of incorrect predictions, and describe the annotation procedure. Each incorrect answer is assigned the single error type that most directly leads to the chosen option: Visual Grounding Error. The model misidentifies what or who is involved. For example, it confuses or overlooks an object or scene element, or attributes the action to another visible person instead of the camera wearer. Motion and Body-State Perception Error. The model misperceives what the wearers own body does, such as their locomotion, movement direction, posture, the limb used, or the action performed, as well as body actions it fails to notice at all. Temporal Localization Error. The model recognizes the relevant events but places them wrongly in time. For instance, it anchors on the wrong moment or reverses their order. Prior-Driven Inference. The answer follows from expectation rather than evidence, such as procedural common sense, default assumptions, reinterpreted question or option wording, or assumptions about the dataset, and may rely on observations invented to support that expectation. Since manually reading all 400 long reasoning traces is extremely labor-intensive, we combined automated labeling with manual verification, following similar approaches in the literature (Yang et al., 2026a; Nagrani et al., 2025). Moreover, every clip in SOMA comes with ground-truth atomic action and motion narration annotations, so each claim in reasoning trace can be compared with the annotated ground truth. We therefore used LLM judges: given the question, the judge compares the models reasoning and chosen answer against the ground-truth annotations, together with the correct answer, and assigns one of the four error types, quoting the excerpt of the reasoning that shows the error. To ensure that the labels do not depend on the biases of single judge, we used two judges from different model families, GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, each labeling all 400 traces independently. The agreement between the two judges is high, as they assign the same error type to 80.0% of the traces (Cohens κ = 0.69, 95% bootstrap CI 0.630.75). We additionally verified sample of the labels manually against the video clip and ground-truth annotations and found the assigned types and the quoted evidence consistent with the definitions above.

E.1 QA GENERATION Our training dataset, SOMA-Train, comprises aligned egocentric video and body motion, designed to investigate whether body-motion supervision helps close the gaps exposed by SOMA. We followed the taxonomy of the benchmark and drew on the same two sources, Nymeria and Ego-Exo4D. In total, SOMA-Train contains 28,596 questions from 1,779 takes (570 from Nymeria and 1,209 from Ego-Exo4D), covering 110.2 hours of aligned egocentric video and body motion. Unlike the evaluation setting, where we removed questions answerable from language priors alone, the training setting introduces an additional failure mode: shortcuts that cannot be exploited zeroshot may become learnable during fine-tuning. We therefore adapted the generation pipeline for SOMA-Train by controlling distractor construction per task, so that the correct option cannot be identified from the question and answer choices alone. When this cannot be guaranteed by construction, we additionally applied adversarial filtering. Together, these steps target training-time bias, i.e., shortcuts learnable from the training distribution itself. We present the pipeline in two parts. We first describe the construction of SOMA-Train in four steps: question templating, task-specific extraction, distractor construction and balancing, and final grammar and factuality verification (Appendix E.1.1). We then test the resulting dataset for training-time bias by measuring whether model trained without video or motion input transfers to SOMA (Appendix E.1.2). E.1.1 CONSTRUCTION Question Templates. For each question, we randomly sampled one of the task-specific templates  (Table 7)  , which follow the question formats of the corresponding SOMA tasks, and filled it with fields extracted from the clip annotation. In the templates, {a} denotes an anchor clause from the annotation (for Missing Event Inference, {a} and {c} denote the surrounding events), {b} the referenced event, {o} the parsed object, {l} the limb pair, {e} the repeated event, and {e1} to {e4} the listed actions. When template has several grammatical variants, we selected the one that matches the form of the extracted anchor. Extraction. The benchmark pipeline uses an LLM selector to identify task-relevant windows in the source annotations. For SOMA-Train, we replaced this step with deterministic task-specific regex-based extractors, which make the extraction fully reproducible and reduce potential sampling biases introduced by LLM-based selection. Each extractor follows phrasing conventions observed in the source annotations and includes task-specific rejection rules for failure cases that we identified throughout the process.

sections.content: Distractor Sampling. As the benchmark follows multiple-choice format, the construction of distractor options is crucial. We designed the distractors separately for each task: we aimed to balance the options by construction, making sure that no candidate is more likely to be correct than another based on the textual information and task-specific category structure alone. We denote the ground-truth answer by g, an option string by s, conditioning context by c, and the number of candidates within that context by k, and use the following strategies. closed option set presents the same four answer options for every question, such that (g s) = 1/4 (Hand Use). Product construction forms fixed set of candidate combinations while keeping the shared movement clause identical across options (Movement Direction). Rotation within conditioning context fixes candidate actions and rotates the correct answer such that (g offered, c) = 1/k within each context (Opposite Motion Discrimination). Exchangeable option sets are formed from four answers from the same take, with the correct answer rotated so that each appears once as the ground truth and three times as distractor (Bimanual Coordination, Concurrent Body-Part State, Missing Event Inference). When balance cannot be guaranteed by construction, we applied adversarial filtering following Le Bras et al. (2020) (Chronological Ordering). Grammar and Factuality Corrections. Templateand regex-based question generation can introduce systematic grammatical and wording artifacts, e.g., incorrect verb forms, subject-verb agreement errors, missing subjects, truncated options, or spelling errors inherited from the source annotations. These artifacts can also introduce shortcuts when they correlate with the correct option or alter the meaning of an answer. We used Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026b) to correct these grammatical and wording artifacts while preserving the original semantic content and avoiding the introduction of new answerspecific biases. We additionally used the same model to verify the generated questions against the original human annotations, correcting or removing examples with remaining inconsistencies. E.1.2 DEBIASING VALIDATION To validate our approach, we measured whether model trained without modality input (motion and/or video) could still exploit learnable signal from the training dataset. Ideally, its performance should remain close to the random baseline, indicating that successful fine-tuning requires relying on task-relevant perceptual information rather than on shortcuts in the training distribution. To this end, we trained the model on the full SOMA-Train set with text input only and evaluated it blind on SOMA  (Table 8)  . We found that blind performance remained close to the random baseline, while the gap between the video+motion variant and the blind model reached +16.65 points. This provides evidence that the observed fine-tuning gains rely on perceptual input rather than on language understanding and distributional shortcuts alone. sections.content: only 2,592 of the 3,634 non-climbing takes, leaving 12.9% of our Ego-Exo4D benchmark questions without body motion. We compared against the released EE4D-Motion dataset (Patel et al., 2025). We therefore reprocessed Ego-Exo4D to obtain denser SMPL-X fits. We followed the multi-view fitting pipeline of EE4D-Motion (Patel et al., 2025), which detects the camera wearer in the exocentric views, estimates 2D keypoints, initializes SMPL-X from single-view reconstruction, and refines the sequence through multi-view reprojection. We kept the same multi-view approach but replaced the single-view pose estimation and reconstruction stages with SAM 3D Body (Yang et al., 2026b). We provide further details below: Detection and Subject Selection. We detected people with RF-DETR (Robinson et al., 2025) and identified the camera wearer by projecting the Aria trajectory into each exocentric view and selecting the nearest detection. We re-detected when the tracked box moved too far from the projected Aria position. We set this threshold independently for each camera to 2.5 times its median head-to-anchor distance, clamped to [60, 250] px. This trajectory-based association is important in scenes containing multiple people, where tracking based only on the detected person can switch to bystander. Per-view Pose Estimation. We applied SAM 3D Body independently to each selected view. The model jointly predicts 2D and 3D keypoints, body parameters, and camera parameters, allowing both the keypoints and body initialization to come from the same model. We ran this stage at 20 fps. Triangulation. We undistorted the predicted keypoints using each cameras KannalaBrandt fisheye model and triangulated them using the Ego-Exo4D GoPro calibration. We required at least two valid views and removed joints with reprojection residual above 60 px. We used the calibration stored in the take trajectory. Multi-view Fitting. We jointly optimized one SMPL-X sequence across all available views, with body shape shared across the take. Triangulated joints initialize the global orientation and translation. The objective combines robust reprojection loss over the 34 matched joints, agreement with the per-view SAM 3D Body predictions, temporal smoothness, and pose and shape regularization. We additionally removed cameras whose median distance to the selected subject exceeds three times that of the closest camera. Evaluation. We evaluated our fits and EE4D-Motion against the human-verified Ego-Exo4D annotations, which provide 3D keypoints triangulated from manually annotated exocentric views. We regressed both SMPL-X sequences to the same joint set before evaluation. As SAM 3D Body derives its output keypoints from the MHR model (Ferguson et al., 2025), while Ego-Exo4D follows the 17-keypoint COCO convention (Grauman et al., 2024), the error may also include systematic convention mismatch. We corrected this by estimating one constant offset per joint on the training takes and applying the same correction to validation for both methods. To validate our pipeline, we report the reconstruction error on the intersection of takes covered by the annotations, EE4DMotion and our pipeline, averaging first within each take and then across takes. We evaluated with PA-MPJPE because EE4D-Motion refits are defined independently for each window and do not preserve common world coordinate system, which prevents direct comparison of global trajectories. Results. Our fits reached 36.7 mm PA-MPJPE on validation, compared with 40.3 mm for EE4DMotion  (Table 9)  . The joint correction reduced the errors by 5.9 and 3.9 mm, moving our result from 42.6 to 36.7 mm and EE4D-Motion from 44.2 to 40.3 mm, respectively, without changing their ordering. We report the training results for completeness, although the offsets are fitted on the training takes. Coverage. Following EE4D-Motion, we excluded Rock Climbing because our motion representation expresses height relative to the floor. Although this removes 1,401 of the 5,035 takes, these account for only 17.1 of 221.3 video hours. Of the remaining 3,634 takes, our pipeline fitted 3,475, corresponding to 190.7 of 204.1 hours. The remaining 159 takes have missing source data. We measured coverage over the original 30 fps video timeline while accounting for the native sampling rate of each motion source. Our fits covered 93.1% of the training video and 96.2% of validation, compared with 70.5% and 73.1% for EE4D-Motion  (Table 10)  .

We extended two open-weight backbones, Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025) and InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025), with body-motion pathway following the standard LLaVA/- MotionLLM design (Liu et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2026). motion encoder maps each motion sequence to sequence of continuous features, which trainable MLP projects into the language-model embedding space. The projected features are inserted into the input sequence as motion tokens. Motion encoder. We used the convolutional encoder of VQ-VAE (Zhang et al., 2023) that operates on 263-dimensional body-motion features (Guo et al., 2022). The VQ-VAE was trained for reconstruction on 156,659 motion clips from the SOMA-Train takes of Nymeria and Ego-Exo4D, sampled as 64-frame windows at 20 fps. We used its continuous pre-quantization features, one per 4 frames. The encoder was kept frozen throughout all subsequent training steps.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Training overview. We compared video-only, motion-only, and video+motion variants. Motionbased variants were trained in two stages: we first aligned the motion projector on motionnarration pairs, then fine-tuned the language model on SOMA-Train with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022). We skipped Stage 1 for the video-only variant since the backbones already include pretrained vision encoder and projector, and fine-tuned each backbone on SOMA-Train using video input only. Stage 1: Motionlanguage alignment. We aligned the motion modality using the motionnarration annotations of the Nymeria takes in SOMA-Train (Ma et al., 2024). We rewrote each narration into three body-part descriptions (legs and feet, arms and hands, overall posture), each treated as separate target, resulting in 24,549 samples from 8,183 clips. The model received motion as the only input, and only the projector was trained while the language model remained frozen. We trained for one epoch with learning rate of 103, cosine schedule with warmup ratio of 0.03, and global batch size of 16. Stage 2: Question answering. All variants were fine-tuned on SOMA-Train with LoRA (rank 128, α = 256, dropout 0.05) applied to the language model. For motion-based variants, we initialized from the Stage 1 projector and kept it frozen. We trained for two epochs with LoRA learning rate of 5 105, using the same schedule and warmup as Stage 1, gradient clipping at 1.0, and bf16 precision with gradient checkpointing. Training ran on 8 H100 GPUs with per-device batch size of 6 (global batch size 48). E.4 ADDITIONAL RESULTS To analyze how the contribution of motion varies across task types, we examined per-task results  (Table 11)  . Adding motion to video improves both backbones on Body Posture, Opposite Motion Discrimination, Missing Event Inference, and Next Action Prediction, while hurting both on Hand Use and Adjacent Action Identification. This suggests that the effect of motion depends largely on what each task requires: motion helps when body state or movement carries information that is hard to recover from video alone. When the evidence is already visible in the video, however, motion tokens add little new information and may instead introduce redundant or noisy signals that distract the model from the relevant visual evidence.
